summary: The village of the men who cut and painted the royal tombs, and the best-documented ordinary people of the ancient world.
look: Below you lie the stone footings of about 68 houses packed inside a wall that follows the shape of the narrow valley, with one street running north to south down the middle. The workmen's own tombs climb the western slope, some still topped with small mud-brick pyramids. At the north end stands the little Ptolemaic temple of Hathor inside its brick enclosure.
story:
The village was called Set Maat, the Place of Truth, and its men were the Servants in the Place of Truth: the crew who cut, plastered and painted the tombs in the Valley of the Kings. The earliest datable remains belong to the reign of Thutmose I, and the villagers honoured Amenhotep I and his mother Ahmose-Nefertari as divine patrons for generations. The village was abandoned under Ramesses XI, around 1110-1080 BC, amid tomb robberies, Libyan raids and civil war.

The crew was split into two gangs, the left side and the right side, each with a foreman, and a scribe kept the records. They worked eight days and rested two, sleeping in stone huts on the pass above the Valley during the working week. The state paid them in grain and other rations. The nearest well was about half an hour's walk away, so water carriers kept the village supplied.

What makes Deir el-Medina special is its paperwork. Villagers wrote on ostraca, flakes of limestone and broken pottery, and thousands survive: about 5,000 came from a single shaft near the village. There are laundry lists, sick notes, accusations, prayers, love poems and school exercises. A large part of the community, perhaps including some women, could read, so we know their names, their debts and their quarrels.

A typical house covered about 70 square metres: an entrance room, often with a raised brick platform in one corner, perhaps a shrine or a bed for childbirth, then a main room, two small rooms, a kitchen with a cellar and a stair to the roof. Windows sat high to keep out the sun. Bernard Bruyere's French team excavated the whole site between 1922 and 1951.
details: The main street: walk it from north to south and count the doorways; each house is a long, narrow strip.
Entrance rooms: look for the raised brick platform in a corner, the so-called lit clos, perhaps a shrine or a birthing bed.
The western slope: the workmen's tomb chapels, a few with little restored mud-brick pyramids on top.
The footpath climbing the hill to the north-west: the workmen's weekly commute over the mountain to the Valley of the Kings.
Cellars: small sunken spaces at the back of some houses, where food and valuables were kept cool.
fun_fact: The villagers' favourite judge was a king who had been dead for centuries: the statue of the deified Amenhotep I gave oracles that settled their quarrels over property and theft.
narration: Below you is the village of the men who made the royal tombs. Its ancient name was Set Maat, the Place of Truth. For about four centuries, some 70 families lived inside this wall, along one narrow street. The men cut, plastered and painted the tombs in the Valley of the Kings, just over the hill. They worked in two gangs, the left side and the right side, each with a foreman, and a scribe kept the books. They worked eight days, rested two, and slept in huts up on the pass during the working week. The state paid them in grain. The nearest well was half an hour away, so water carriers brought it up by donkey. What makes this place famous is the paperwork. Villagers scribbled on flakes of limestone and broken pots called ostraca, and thousands survive: laundry lists, sick notes, lawsuits, love poems and school exercises. So we know their names, their debts and their quarrels better than almost anyone else's in the ancient world. Walk down the main street and step into a house. The front room often has a raised brick platform in the corner, perhaps a shrine, perhaps a bed for giving birth. Behind it is the main room, then a kitchen with a cellar and a stair to the roof. Now look up at the western slope. Those doorways are the workmen's own tombs, a few still topped with little brick pyramids.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II, early 13th century BC
summary: Found sealed in 1886: a tomb painter's own family vault, where he and his wife plough and harvest forever in the fields of paradise.
look: A steep stair takes you down into a single small vaulted burial chamber, painted on every surface over a warm yellow ground. The Field of Reeds fills the east end wall under its arched top; Anubis tending the mummy is on the north long wall, and the vault is divided into panels of gods and the sky goddess in her sycamore tree. Above ground, Sennedjem's small pyramid chapel has been restored to almost 7 m.
story:
Sennedjem was a Servant in the Place of Truth under Seti I and Ramesses II, one of the craftsmen who decorated the royal tombs. Here the same team worked for one of their own, and you can feel the care. His wife Iyneferti, a singer of Hathor, gave him at least ten children; the eldest, Khabekhnet, has the tomb next door.

In January 1886 a local man, Salam Abu Duhi, and three companions found the chamber still sealed. Eduardo Toda cleared it for Gaston Maspero and counted about 165 objects. At least 20 people lay inside, nine of them in coffins. Everything went to the museum in Cairo, and much was then sold to fund excavations: the Metropolitan Museum in New York bought the mummies and coffins of Iyneferti and their son Khonsu, Berlin bought others. Sennedjem's own coffins stayed in Cairo and are now at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization. The painted wooden door, with the couple playing senet on its inner face, is also in Cairo.

The decoration runs from west to east, like the journey of the dead towards rebirth. On the east wall is the goal: the Field of Reeds, the paradise of the Book of the Dead. Sennedjem and Iyneferti, in white linen, plough with a pair of cows, sow and cut tall grain, among palms and fruit trees on an island ringed by canals. It is a farmer's heaven: the reward for a good life is more farming, in perfect weather. Above them, baboons greet the rising sun in its boat.
details: East wall: the couple ploughing, sowing and reaping in the Field of Reeds, ringed by blue canals.
Arched top of the east wall: baboons raising their arms to the rising sun in its boat.
Doorway: Ra as a cat with a knife, cutting off the head of the serpent Apophis.
North wall: Anubis bending over Sennedjem's mummy on its bed, inside the embalming tent.
Ceiling vault: the sky goddess as a sycamore tree, offering food and drink to the couple.
fun_fact: The burial survived intact for over 3,000 years, then was scattered within a few years of its discovery; one coffin bought by Berlin was destroyed by bombing in 1945.
narration: You are inside the burial chamber of Sennedjem, a craftsman who decorated royal tombs under Seti the First and Ramesses the Second. His title was Servant in the Place of Truth. Here, for once, he and his colleagues worked for one of their own, and you can feel the care. In January 1886 a local man, Salam Abu Duhi, and three friends found this chamber still sealed. Inside lay at least 20 members of the family, with coffins, furniture and tools. It all went to the museum in Cairo, and much of it was then sold: the coffins of his wife Iyneferti and his son Khonsu are now in New York. Now look at the end wall with the golden fields. This is the Field of Reeds, the paradise of the Book of the Dead. Sennedjem and Iyneferti, in fine white linen, plough with a pair of cows, sow the seed and cut tall grain, on an island ringed by blue canals, among palms and fruit trees. It is a farmer's heaven: the reward for a good life is more farming, but in perfect weather. Above them, baboons greet the rising sun in its boat. On one long wall, Anubis bends over Sennedjem's mummy on its bed. Before you climb out, look at the doorway: a cat holding a knife is cutting off the head of the serpent Apophis, the enemy of the sun.

summary: A tomb painter's own burial vault, where he kneels by a pool under a palm tree to drink in the next world.
look: A very steep, narrow stair leads down to a small vaulted burial chamber, so keep a hand on the rail. Black jackals of Anubis guard the doorway. On the end wall Osiris sits enthroned with Pashedu kneeling before him; the scene of Pashedu drinking under the palm tree is the other image to find.
story:
Pashedu was a Servant in the Place of Truth, a member of the royal tomb crew, the son of Menna and Huy; his wife was called Nedjemet-behdet. The name Pashedu was common in the village, and several men who bore it appear in the records, so it is hard to pin down exactly when this one lived. He also owned a second tomb nearby, TT326.

Like his neighbour Sennedjem, he dug a family vault below a small chapel on the slope and decorated it with the skill he used for kings.

The picture everyone remembers shows Pashedu kneeling beside a pool under a palm tree heavy with fruit, bending to drink. In a desert country, cool water in the afterlife was a serious matter, and the Book of the Dead has spells to guarantee it.

On the end wall Osiris sits on his throne, with Pashedu kneeling in prayer. Behind him an Eye of Horus, given a pair of human arms, holds out a vessel, perhaps a lamp, and beyond it stands a falcon. Elsewhere a row of gods holds the ankh, the sign of life, and the family lines up to share Pashedu's eternity.
details: The doorway: the two black jackals of Anubis lying on guard.
The palm-tree scene: Pashedu kneeling to drink from a pool under a tree loaded with fruit.
End wall: Osiris enthroned, Pashedu kneeling, and the Eye of Horus with human arms holding out a vessel.
Upper left wall: a row of seated gods, each holding an ankh.
fun_fact: The Eye of Horus here has grown arms: the painters turned a symbol into a character who can hand things to the gods.
narration: Mind the stairs: the way down is steep and narrow. You are in the burial vault of Pashedu, a member of the royal tomb crew who lived in the village below. Like his neighbour Sennedjem, he painted for kings and then, in his own time, painted for himself. As you go in, two black jackals of the god Anubis watch the doorway. Now look for the picture that made this tomb famous. Pashedu kneels beside a pool under a palm tree heavy with fruit, and bends down to drink. In a desert country, cool water in the afterlife mattered, and the Book of the Dead had spells to make sure you got it. On the end wall, Osiris, king of the dead, sits on his throne. Pashedu kneels in prayer before him. Behind Pashedu stands an Eye of Horus that has grown a pair of human arms, holding out an offering to the god, and beyond it a falcon. Along the walls, rows of gods hold the ankh, the sign of life, and Pashedu's family line up to share his eternity. As you climb back up, look again at the jackals over the door: they are still on duty after more than 3,000 years.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, reigns of Ramesses III and Ramesses IV
summary: The tomb of a foreman of the royal tomb crew, painted when the village's artists were at their best: a harpist, a knife-wielding cat and rows of kings.
look: Steps lead down to two small chambers, one behind the other, painted with large figures on a yellow ground. In the outer chamber, Inherkhau and his wife Wab stand before two rows of kings, queens and princes. Look for the harpist, the cat slaying the serpent and the Bennu heron among the panels.
story:
Inherkhau held the title Foreman of the Lord of the Two Lands in the Place of Truth. He was one of the two men who ran the gangs cutting the royal tombs, under Ramesses III and Ramesses IV, the years of the great strikes. His father Huy had been foreman before him. His wife Wab and his sons Kenna and Harmin appear with him on the walls. He also owned a second tomb, TT299.

A foreman could call on the best painters in Egypt, and here they worked at full stretch.

The most unusual scene is in the outer chamber: Inherkhau and Wab adore two rows of kings, queens and princes, the Lords of the West. They are led by the village's patron saints, King Amenhotep I and his mother Queen Ahmose-Nefertari, who had been dead for more than three centuries. A scene of the same pair from the inner doorway is now in Berlin.

Elsewhere a harpist sings to the couple, the Bennu heron, the soul of the sun god, stands before Inherkhau, and Thoth escorts him towards Osiris. The outer chamber also carries texts from the Book of Gates and the Book of the Dead.
details: Outer chamber: Inherkhau and Wab before two rows of royal ancestors, the Lords of the West.
The harpist playing and singing for the seated couple.
Ra as a great cat with a knife, slicing the head off the serpent Apophis.
The Bennu heron, a grey bird with a long crest, standing before Inherkhau.
Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, leading Inherkhau towards Osiris.
fun_fact: Inherkhau's father was a foreman too: running the royal tomb gangs was something of a family business in Deir el-Medina.
narration: This is the burial of Inherkhau, a foreman of the royal tomb crew under Ramesses the Third and his son Ramesses the Fourth, the years of the great strikes. His father had been foreman before him. A foreman could call on the best painters in Egypt, and here you see them at full stretch: big, confident figures on a golden ground. In the outer chamber, find Inherkhau and his wife Wab praying before two rows of kings, queens and princes. These are the Lords of the West, led by the village's patron saints, King Amenhotep the First and his mother, Queen Ahmose-Nefertari, dead for more than three centuries by then. Elsewhere, a harpist sings to the couple, and the heron called the Bennu, the soul of the sun, stands before Inherkhau. Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe of the gods, leads him towards Osiris. Then find the fiercest image in the tomb: the sun god as a great cat, holding a knife, slicing off the head of the serpent Apophis. Every night, the Egyptians believed, that fight decided whether the sun would rise again.

period: Ptolemaic, begun under Ptolemy IV (221-204 BC); later a monastery
summary: A small Ptolemaic temple of Hathor and Maat that became the monastery behind the site's name, with a rare judgement-of-the-dead scene inside.
look: At the north end of the village a tall mud-brick enclosure wall surrounds a compact sandstone temple: a small columned hall, then three sanctuaries side by side. In one of them the weighing of the heart covers a side wall. The Great Pit, a deep shaft, lies just outside the enclosure.
story:
Long after the workmen had gone, the Ptolemies built a temple here, on the site of an older shrine to Hathor, goddess of the western mountain who welcomed the dead. It was begun under Ptolemy IV Philopator, the Macedonian king who won the battle of Raphia, and finished by his successors. It honours Hathor together with Maat, goddess of truth and order: a fitting pair for the old Place of Truth.

In Christian times the temple became the Monastery of Saint Isidorus the Martyr. The Arabic name Deir el-Medina, the monastery of the town, comes from it, so the whole village is named after its last tenants.

Inside, one chapel carries a scene usually painted on papyrus and rarely carved on a temple wall: the judgement of the dead from chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead. Osiris presides. The heart is weighed against the feather of Maat. Thoth writes down the verdict, and Ammut, part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus, waits to eat the heart of the guilty.

Just outside lies the Great Pit, a shaft about 50 m deep, apparently dug in search of water it never reached. The villagers used it as a dump, and when Bernard Bruyere's team emptied it, it yielded thousands of ostraca.
details: The judgement scene: the scales, the feather, Thoth with his writing palette and Ammut waiting.
Columned hall: Hathor faces and the cow-eared goddess on the reliefs.
The mud-brick enclosure wall, still standing to almost its full height around the temple.
Outside the enclosure: the fenced Great Pit, source of thousands of written notes.
fun_fact: The whole workmen's village takes its modern name from Christian monks who moved into a Greek king's temple a thousand years after the workmen had left.
narration: This little temple, the youngest building here, gave the whole village its name. Ptolemy the Fourth, one of the Macedonian Greek kings of Egypt, began it on the site of an older shrine to Hathor. It honours her together with Maat, goddess of truth, a good match for a village once called the Place of Truth. Centuries later, Christian monks moved in and made it a monastery, a deir in Arabic. That is why the site is called Deir el-Medina, the monastery of the town. Inside, look for a scene that is rare on temple walls: the judgement of the dead. The heart of the dead lies on one pan of a scale, the feather of truth on the other, and Thoth writes down the result. Ammut, part crocodile, part lion, part hippo, waits to eat any heart that fails. Just outside is the Great Pit, a shaft about 50 metres deep. The villagers used it as a rubbish dump, and archaeologists pulled thousands of written notes out of it. Find the scales on the wall and check that they are perfectly level: that was the verdict everyone hoped for.

period: New Kingdom, 19th-20th Dynasties; the strike in year 29 of Ramesses III, c. 1157 BC
summary: When their grain was late, the royal tomb builders put down their tools and sat down outside the temples: the first strike on record.
look: This is a story rather than a monument. Stand on the village street, or by the Great Pit at the north end, where thousands of the notes that tell it were found. The strike papyrus itself is in the Egyptian Museum in Turin; the ostraca are scattered between Cairo, Paris, London, Berlin and many other collections.
story:
In year 29 of Ramesses III, around 1157 BC, the monthly grain rations that paid the tomb crew were late, and not for the first time. Egypt's economy was under strain after the wars of the reign. The scribe Amennakht recorded what happened next on a papyrus now in Turin. The men downed tools, walked out past the guard posts of the necropolis and sat down behind the temple of Thutmose III on the edge of the fields. They told the officials they had come because of hunger and thirst, with no clothes, no oil, no fish and no vegetables. Eventually the rations came. When they lapsed again, the men walked out again. It is the first strike recorded in history.

The story survives because this village wrote everything down, on ostraca: flakes of limestone and broken pots. One absence register from the reign of Ramesses II reads like a sick-leave sheet: a man brewing beer, another stung by a scorpion, one embalming his brother, one whose wife was bleeding. The village also had a physician and a scorpion charmer.

There are love songs, letters, hymns, wills and lawsuits. The villain of the archive is Paneb, son of an overseer, accused of looting royal tombs, adultery and stirring up trouble; we never learn his fate. An old woman named Naunakhte left a will that disinherited the children who had not looked after her.

How many villagers could read is still argued, but clearly many could, probably including some women. At the very end of the New Kingdom the papyri change tone: they record trials of tomb robbers, as the state that paid these men fell apart.
details: Great Pit, beyond the Hathor temple: the rubbish shaft that became the village archive.
White limestone flakes on the ground around you: the villagers' notepaper. Please leave them where they lie.
Look east from the village towards the fields: the strikers walked down to the temples on the edge of the cultivation.
The path over the hill to the Valley of the Kings: workmen scratched their names on rocks along the way.
fun_fact: The scribe's absence register reads like an office sick-leave sheet: 'brewing beer', 'stung by a scorpion', 'embalming his brother'.
narration: This stop is about people, and the notes they left. In year 29 of King Ramesses the Third, around 1157 BC, the grain that paid the tomb builders was late again. The men of this village put down their tools, walked out past the guard posts and sat down behind the royal temple of Thutmose the Third, on the edge of the fields. They told the officials they had come because of hunger and thirst: no clothes, no oil, no fish, no vegetables. The scribe Amennakht wrote it all down, and his papyrus, now in Turin, is the first record of a strike in history. It worked, at least for a while: the rations came. When they stopped, the men walked out again. We know so much because these people wrote on everything. Papyrus was expensive, so they used flakes of limestone and broken pots, called ostraca. One register lists why men missed work: brewing beer, a scorpion sting, embalming a brother, a wife who was bleeding. There are love songs, letters, wills and lawsuits. There is a villain, the foreman Paneb, accused of robbing a royal tomb, threatening his colleagues and sleeping with their wives. There is an old woman, Naunakhte, who cut her ungrateful children out of her will. Before you leave, look at the white limestone flakes on the ground around you. That was their notepaper. Please leave them where they are.

summary: Ta-Set-Neferu, the Place of Beauty: around a hundred tombs of queens, princes and princesses, and the finest painted tomb in Egypt.
look: A narrow desert wadi with doorways cut into both sides, each marked with a QV number. The path runs up the main valley past the open tombs; Nefertari's tomb, QV66, has its own shelter, separate ticket and timed visit. Only a few tombs open at a time, usually including the princes' tombs QV55 and QV44 and Queen Tyti's QV52.
story:
The ancient name was Ta-Set-Neferu, usually translated the Place of Beauty, though it can also mean the Place of the Royal Children. The main wadi holds 91 tombs and its side valleys another 19 or so.

The first burials, in the 18th Dynasty, were simple shafts and chambers for princes, princesses and officials. One of the earliest belongs to Princess Ahmose, daughter of King Seqenenre Tao. In the 19th Dynasty the valley was reserved for royal women. Queen Satre, wife of Ramesses I, probably has the first of these tombs, QV38, and the great wives of Seti I and Ramesses II followed, Nefertari among them. Some tombs were cut in advance without a name, ready for the next royal woman to die. Under Ramesses III royal sons were buried here too, which is why you will see the king leading little princes before the gods. Work went on at least until Ramesses VI.

Why here? Nobody knows for certain. The valley is close to the workmen's village, and a grotto in the valley was sacred to Hathor, goddess of the west and of rebirth. In rare rainstorms water pours over the cliffs at the end of the valley, and one theory links the grotto and that water with the goddess.

After the New Kingdom the tombs were robbed and reused, filled with burials again in Roman times, and lived in by Christian hermits until about the 7th century. Ernesto Schiaparelli and Francesco Ballerini of the Turin museum explored the valley from 1903, which is why so many finds from here are in Turin.
details: Tomb doorways on both sides of the path, each with its QV number: there are 91 in this main valley alone.
QV66, Nefertari: look for the shelter and the separate ticket check.
QV55 and QV44: the princes' tombs of Ramesses III's sons, bright and usually quiet.
The cliffs at the end of the wadi, where water pours down after the rare storms.
fun_fact: Some tombs here were cut before anyone needed them, with a blank where the name should go: ready-made eternity, waiting for the next queen.
narration: Welcome to the Valley of the Queens. The Egyptians called it Ta-Set-Neferu, usually translated the Place of Beauty, though it can also mean the Place of the Royal Children. There are 91 tombs in this main valley, and about 20 more in the side valleys. The first burials, about 3,500 years ago, were simple shafts for princes, princesses and court officials. Then, under the kings of Dynasty 19, the valley was kept for royal wives. Queen Satre, wife of Ramesses the First, probably had the first of these tombs, and the great queens of Seti the First and Ramesses the Second followed, Nefertari among them. Some tombs were even cut in advance, with a blank space where a name would go, waiting for the next royal woman to die. Under Ramesses the Third, little princes were buried here too, and in their tombs you will see the king holding his son's hand and introducing him to the gods. Why this valley? Nobody knows for sure. It is close to the workmen's village, and a grotto here was sacred to Hathor, the goddess who welcomed the dead into the western mountain. Later the tombs were robbed, reused for Roman burials, and lived in by Christian hermits. An Italian team from the Turin museum explored the valley from 1903. As you walk up the path, read the signs by each doorway: Q V, for Queens' Valley, and the tomb number.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses II, c. 1279-1213 BC
summary: The tomb of Ramesses II's best-loved queen, painted like a jewel box: many think it is the most beautiful tomb in Egypt.
look: A rock-cut staircase takes you down to an antechamber with a side room, then a second stair leads to the burial hall, about 90 square metres, with four painted pillars. Ceilings are dark blue with yellow five-pointed stars. The figures are carved in plaster laid over the rock, then painted. The visit is short and strictly timed, so decide in advance what you want to see.
story:
Nefertari was the great royal wife of Ramesses II, his favourite by every sign. He built the smaller temple at Abu Simbel in her honour, which you saw on the 17th, and she exchanged letters and gifts with the Hittite queen Puduhepa.

Ernesto Schiaparelli found the tomb in 1904, in his second season in the valley: steps under the rubble led down to a doorway with the queen's name. Robbers had got there first, probably in antiquity. They left fragments of a pink granite sarcophagus lid, about thirty shabtis, palm-fibre sandals, linen and parts of a pair of legs. The knee fragments are in Turin, and a 2016 scientific study concluded that they very probably belong to the queen.

The rock here is poor, cracked limestone, so the artists laid plaster over it, carved the figures into the plaster and painted them. About 520 square metres of painting cover the walls. Salt crystals and water seeping into the rock pushed the plaster away, and the tomb was closed in 1950. From 1986 to 1992 the Getty Conservation Institute and the Egyptian Antiquities Organisation stabilised and cleaned every surface. They repainted nothing: what was lost stays lost. Access has been limited ever since.

The walls follow the queen's journey through the Book of the Dead. She plays senet alone in a pavilion, from chapter 17. She asks Thoth for his water bowl and scribe's palette, from chapter 94. Isis leads her by the hand. On the way down she passes the guarded gates of Osiris's kingdom, and in the burial hall she stands among the gods, ready for eternity.
details: Antechamber, west wall: Nefertari playing senet in a pavilion, then the Bennu heron and two lions holding up the horizon.
Ceilings: dark blue sky with yellow five-pointed stars.
Side room: the seven heavenly cows and their bull above four steering oars, and the queen before Thoth.
Burial hall pillars: Horus as a priest in a leopard skin, and Anubis and Hathor receiving the queen.
Her face: soft red shading on the cheeks, rare in Egyptian painting, and transparent white linen.
fun_fact: After it reopened in the 1990s, access was later cut so hard that in 2006 a private visit for up to 20 people cost 3,000 US dollars.
narration: You are inside the tomb of Nefertari, great royal wife of Ramesses the Second, and many people think it is the most beautiful painted tomb in Egypt. Ramesses adored her. He built the smaller temple at Abu Simbel in her honour, which you saw on the 17th, and she even exchanged letters with the queen of the Hittites. When the Italian archaeologist Ernesto Schiaparelli found this tomb in 1904, robbers had got there first, probably in antiquity. They left a few shabti figures, a pair of sandals and fragments of her legs; in 2016 scientists concluded the knees were very probably hers. The rock here is poor limestone, so the artists covered it with plaster, carved the figures into the plaster and painted them. Salt and water later pushed the plaster off the walls. From 1986 to 1992 conservators from the Getty Institute and Egypt saved every flake, but they repainted nothing. What you see is original. Look up first: a dark blue sky full of yellow five-pointed stars. In the first room, find Nefertari sitting alone in a pavilion, playing the board game senet against an invisible opponent. In another scene the goddess Isis takes her by the hand and leads her on. Then look at the queen herself: the transparent white linen, the vulture headdress, and the soft red shading on her cheeks.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses III, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: A king holding his son's hand and introducing him to god after god: Ramesses III and the prince Amunherkhepshef, in colours still fresh.
look: A ramp leads down to an antechamber, a corridor and a rear chamber holding the prince's pink granite sarcophagus. The paint is bright blue, red and yellow on white: the tall figure is Ramesses III, the small one behind him with the sidelock is the prince. In a glass case in a side room lies a small mummified foetus, brought here from another tomb.
story:
Amunherkhepshef, whose name means Amun is with his strong arm, was a son of Ramesses III. He seems to have been the heir for a time: after his death his father named the future Ramesses IV as successor. Guides often say he died aged about nine, but nothing in the tomb tells us his age. He is drawn with the sidelock of youth, the mark of a royal child.

Schiaparelli found the tomb in 1904, its entrance still partly walled up. Inside were only a few objects and an unfinished sarcophagus. One side room was plastered but never painted.

The walls tell a simple story. The boy cannot face the gods alone, so his father leads him. The king offers and speaks to Isis, Hathor, Shu and others; the prince follows. The king even takes the hand of Qebehsenuef, one of the four sons of Horus. In the corridor stand four knife-carrying guardians of the gates of Osiris's kingdom, from chapter 145 of the Book of the Dead. Isis and Nephthys welcome him at the door of the burial chamber.

The mummified foetus came from a tomb in the side valley of Prince Ahmose and was placed here around 1974. Romantic stories link it to the prince's family; there is no evidence for them.
details: Antechamber, south wall: Ramesses III with Isis on the left and with Hathor on the right, the prince behind him.
Antechamber, west wall: the king holding the hand of Qebehsenuef, one of the sons of Horus.
Corridor: four gate guardians with knives, from the Book of the Dead.
Door to the rear chamber: Isis and Nephthys kneeling to welcome the prince; inside, the pink granite sarcophagus.
fun_fact: Schiaparelli found this tomb by following the remains of an ancient dam across the wadi, built to steer flash floods away from the tombs.
narration: Here a father walks his son into eternity. The tall figure is Ramesses the Third. The small one following him, with the long sidelock of hair worn by royal children, is his son Amunherkhepshef, whose name means Amun is with his strong arm. He seems to have been heir to the throne for a time, but he died young. Guides say he was nine; in truth nobody knows. Since a boy could not face the gods alone, his father does the talking. On wall after wall the king introduces his son: to Isis, to Hathor, to Shu. In one scene he even holds the hand of a god, one of the four sons of Horus who guarded the organs of the dead. In the corridor stand gatekeepers of the underworld, armed with knives, who would only let the boy pass if he knew their names. And the little mummified foetus in the glass case? It was brought here from another tomb in the 1970s and has nothing to do with the prince. Before you leave, compare the two figures again: the king in his tall crown, and the boy, half his height, always one step behind.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses III, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: Another son of Ramesses III, following his father past the gods and the guardians of the underworld: bright, peaceful and usually uncrowded.
look: An unusually wide corridor with two side rooms leads to a second corridor and the burial chamber at the back. Ramesses III, in his tall crown, faces the gods; the prince Khaemwaset follows behind him. In the second corridor the prince appears as a priest in a leopard skin.
story:
Do not confuse him with the famous Khaemwaset, son of Ramesses II, the priest of Ptah at Memphis sometimes called the first Egyptologist for restoring old pyramids. This Khaemwaset was a son of Ramesses III, who copied so much from Ramesses II, down to the names of his sons. Several of his sons have tombs here, decorated to a common plan.

The Italian mission found the tomb on 15 February 1903, in its first season. Francesco Ballerini wrote two days later that Schiaparelli and Howard Carter, then the government's inspector of antiquities for Upper Egypt, were sent for and came at once. The team crawled in through an opening and found a room crammed with coffins and mummies thrown together: more than forty wooden coffins of the 25th and 26th Dynasties, laid here about five centuries after the prince. His own granite sarcophagus was still in the burial chamber, broken at the bottom; its outer lid is in Turin.

In the first corridor, the king stands before Ptah, Thoth, Anubis, Ra-Horakhty, Geb and other gods. The side rooms show the four sons of Horus with Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serket. In the second corridor the prince wears the leopard skin of an Iunmutef priest, among the gates of the underworld and their guardians.
details: First corridor: Ramesses III before Ptah, Thoth, Anubis and Ra-Horakhty, with his son behind him.
Side rooms: the four sons of Horus with the goddesses Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serket.
Second corridor: the prince as an Iunmutef priest in a leopard skin.
The prince's sidelock: a single curl of hair hanging at the side of his head.
fun_fact: One of the first people called in to see this tomb, in 1903, was a young inspector named Howard Carter, 19 years before Tutankhamun.
narration: This is the tomb of Prince Khaemwaset, a son of Ramesses the Third. Do not mix him up with the more famous Khaemwaset, son of Ramesses the Second, who restored old pyramids and is sometimes called the first Egyptologist. The Italian team found this tomb on 15 February 1903 and sent for the local antiquities inspector, a young Englishman named Howard Carter, who came at once. Inside were more than 40 wooden coffins, burials added about five centuries after the prince. The decoration is pure Ramesses the Third. In the first corridor the king, in his tall crown, faces Ptah, Thoth, Anubis and other gods, while the boy follows behind him. In the side rooms, the four sons of Horus stand guard with the goddesses Isis and Nephthys. Further in, the prince appears as a priest in a leopard skin, among the gates of the underworld and their guardians. Notice the colours: deep blue, red and yellow, still fresh. And look for the prince's sidelock, a single curl of hair at the side of his head.

summary: A Ramesside queen's tomb in soft, faded colours, where Hathor as a cow steps out of the western mountain to welcome her.
look: A ramp and a corridor lead into a main chamber with three small rooms opening off it, in the shape of a cross. The colours are paler and more worn than in the princes' tombs. In one side room, a tree goddess pours water for the queen, and next to her the Hathor cow emerges from the mountain.
story:
Queen Tyti, also spelled Titi, was king's daughter, king's sister, king's wife and king's mother. Most Egyptologists think she was a wife of Ramesses III and the mother of Ramesses IV.

Her tomb has been open since at least the early 19th century: Belzoni came in 1816 and Champollion in 1828-29. A tomb-robbery papyrus in the British Museum records a man named Nesamun testifying about the looting of a queen's burial, probably this one. Schiaparelli's team cleared it in 1903-04 and found 34 fragments of her granite sarcophagus.

In the antechamber the queen shakes a sistrum before Ptah, Thoth, Ra-Horakhty and Atum. In the rear room Osiris sits enthroned. Conservators worked here in 2006-08.
details: Antechamber: the queen shaking a sistrum, Hathor's rattle, before the gods.
Side room, back wall: the tree goddess pouring water, then Hathor as a cow stepping out of the mountain.
Rear room: Osiris enthroned between Thoth, Nephthys, Neith and Serket.
fun_fact: The tomb has been visited since before hieroglyphs could be read: Champollion himself came here in 1828-29.
narration: This is the tomb of Queen Tyti, also spelled Titi. Her titles cover the whole family: king's daughter, king's sister, king's wife and king's mother. Most Egyptologists think she was a wife of Ramesses the Third and the mother of Ramesses the Fourth. Her burial did not stay safe for long: a papyrus records a man named Nesamun describing the looting of a queen's tomb, probably hers. The paint is paler and more faded than in the princes' tombs, but softer too. In the first room, the queen shakes a sistrum, Hathor's rattle, before the gods. Then find the side room where a cow, the goddess Hathor, steps out of the western mountain to welcome her.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1350 BC
summary: Two 18-metre stone kings who lost their temple, and the one that 'sang' at dawn for Roman tourists, who carved their names on his legs.
look: Two seated statues of Amenhotep III, about 15 m apart, face east-south-east towards the Nile. With their platforms they reach about 18 m. Small figures of his wife Tiye and his mother Mutemwiya stand beside his legs, and on the sides of the thrones the Nile god Hapy ties together the plants of Upper and Lower Egypt. The northern colossus, on your right as you face them, is the one that sang: its upper body is rebuilt in stacked sandstone blocks.
story:
Both giants are Amenhotep III, seated, hands on knees. They stood at the front of his mortuary temple, the largest in Thebes, which has almost entirely vanished behind them. Each weighs an estimated 720 tons. The quartzite was quarried at Gebel el-Ahmar near Cairo and hauled some 675 km to Thebes. A daughter once stood between each king's feet, but those figures are destroyed.

An earthquake in 27 BC broke the northern statue at the waist. Afterwards, within an hour or two of sunrise, it sometimes made a sound, described as a blow, a whistle or a snapping lyre string. The usual explanation is that the warming stone drove out dew trapped in its cracks. Greeks decided the statue was Memnon, the Ethiopian king killed by Achilles at Troy, greeting his mother Eos, the Dawn. The geographer Strabo heard it in 20 BC, though he could not tell whether it came from the statue or from someone in the crowd. In November 130 the Emperor Hadrian and the Empress Sabina came, and the court poet Julia Balbilla carved Greek verses on the leg recording their visits.

Visitors left 107 Greek and Latin inscriptions, dated between AD 20 and 250. The last reliable report of the sound dates to 196. The upper body was later rebuilt in sandstone, traditionally by Septimius Severus around 199, and the voice fell silent, probably because of the weight of the new stone.
details: Beside the king's legs: the small figures of Queen Tiye and of Mutemwiya, the king's mother.
Sides of the thrones: Nile gods binding papyrus and lotus around the hieroglyph for 'unite'.
Northern colossus, legs and feet: Greek and Latin graffiti of Roman visitors, some with dates.
Northern colossus, upper body: the five courses of later sandstone blocks.
Behind them to the west: the excavation of the lost temple, with re-erected statues.
fun_fact: Balbilla's verses suggest Memnon was moody: the imperial party had to come back more than once before he obliged with his song.
narration: In front of you sit two giants, both of them King Amenhotep the Third, carved around 1350 BC to guard the gate of his temple. The temple has almost vanished, but the guards are still on duty. With their platforms they are about 18 metres tall, and each weighs around 720 tons. The stone was quarried near Cairo, about 675 kilometres away. Beside the legs stand small figures of his wife Tiye and his mother Mutemwiya. Then comes the part the Romans loved. In 27 BC an earthquake cracked the northern statue, the one on your right. After that, around sunrise, it sometimes made a sound, a sharp blow or a whistle, probably dew evaporating from the warming stone. Greek visitors decided it was Memnon, the Ethiopian hero killed by Achilles at Troy, calling to his mother, the Dawn. It became one of the great sights of the Roman Empire. The geographer Strabo heard it. In the year 130 the Emperor Hadrian came with the Empress Sabina, and a lady of the court carved Greek poems on the leg to record the visit. More than a hundred Greek and Latin inscriptions are still there, a guestbook nearly 2,000 years old. Later the statue was patched up, traditionally by the Emperor Septimius Severus, and it never sang again. Look at the northern giant now: its upper half is built of stacked blocks, the repair that silenced Memnon.
